drafts.text:
I made an AI roast 30 ChatGPT / Gemini / Claude outputs.

Every single one got destroyed for the same 4 reasons:

1. "In today's world" openers
2. Bullet avalanche where prose should be
3. Hedging language ("might," "could," "potentially")
4. Polite 50-word warmup before the actual point

Not one survivor.

drafts.title: I ran 30 AI-generated texts through an AI roaster. The same 4 flaws appeared in every single output regardless of model.
drafts.text: Spent an afternoon feeding real ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude outputs into a text roast tool to see what patterns came up. Zero outputs escaped unscathed. The 4 things it dinged every time: generic wide-angle openers ("in today's fast-paced..."), over-reliance on bullet lists, epistemic cowardice ("might," "could," "may"), and front-loaded politeness before the actual point. The interesting meta-finding: the best-scoring outputs came from highly specific prompts, not model differences. Full breakdown + the free tool: https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/ai-text-roast/blog/i-made-ai-roast-other-ais-writing-results-were-embarrassingly-accurate-2026/

I just realized: the problem with AI writing isn't the AI. It's the prompt.

I ran 30 AI-generated texts through a roaster this week. Every model got destroyed for the same four things — hedging language, bullet overload, context-free openers, polite filler before the point.

But the outputs that scored best? All had one thing in common: hyper-specific prompts.

"Write a cold email for a 30-person fintech startup's ops lead" outperforms "write a cold email" by an embarrassing margin.

The roaster isn't just feedback on your text. It's a diagnostic on your prompting.

Free tool (paste anything): https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/ai-text-roast/

drafts.title: I ran 200 LinkedIn About sections through an AI buzzword detector. 46% scored D or F. Here's what the top 6% did differently.
drafts.text: Spent a weekend feeding LinkedIn bios into an AI roaster. The grade distribution was brutal: 6% A, 17% B, 31% C, 28% D, 18% F. Senior execs consistently scored WORSE than individual contributors (my theory: they haven't updated in years). The top bios all shared 3 traits: specific claim in first sentence, at least one number in first 80 words, and a human voice — not press release voice. Full breakdown + free tool to check yours: https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/roast-my-bio/blog/i-made-ai-read-200-linkedin-bios-94-percent-corporate-word-salad-2026/

Unpopular opinion: senior people have worse LinkedIn bios than juniors.

I analyzed 200 About sections with an AI buzzword detector. VPs and above scored lower on average than ICs. My theory: they haven't had to re-market themselves in years.

Only 1 in 17 bios earned an A grade. The difference wasn't talent. It was specificity.
